summary: Defines an HTTP response header field called Safe, which a server can use to say that repeating a request is safe. This would let browsers retry some requests, such as certain POSTs, without bothering the user. The document is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: The Safe response header lets a server say whether a client may repeat a request without asking the user first. The memo especially aims to make retries of safe POST requests less disruptive.

subtitle: Defines an HTTP response header that tells clients whether repeating a request is safe.

tldr.problem: HTTP clients have to assume that a POST request is unsafe to repeat, even when repeating it would not cause harmful side effects.
tldr.mechanism: A server can return a Safe header with yes or no to describe whether repeating the same request is safe; a client may repeat a request marked safe without asking the user.
tldr.outcome: Without the header, requests are treated as unsafe except GET and HEAD. Unit metadata classifies RFC 2310 as Historic.

today: RFC 2310 is classified as Historic in the unit metadata. It defines the Safe response header as an experimental addition to HTTP/1.x.

sections.title: Why a Safety Signal Is Useful
sections.content:
HTTP assumes POST requests are unsafe to repeat because they may cause side effects for which the user is responsible. Clients may need to repeat a request after an unclear result, after a reload, or when redisplaying a result from history.

Without a signal from the server, the client must assume a POST is unsafe and ask the user before repeating it. The Safe header gives the server a way to identify requests that can be repeated safely.
sections.plainLanguage: A client may need to send the same request again, but it cannot know whether that could repeat an action. The server's response can tell it when a repeat is safe.

sections.title: The Safe Response Header
sections.content:
The header is written as Safe: yes or Safe: no. A repetition means the same user agent makes a request for the same resource using the same method, with both requests having no body or byte-identical bodies after decoding content and transfer encodings.

If the response has no Safe header, the request is treated as unsafe unless it is GET or HEAD. The header does not change the definition of GET and HEAD as safe methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The header gives a yes-or-no answer for repeating a request. The requests must come from the same client and match in resource, method, and body.

sections.title: How a Client Can Respond
sections.content:
If the response marks a repeated request as safe, a user agent may repeat it automatically without asking for confirmation. If the header is missing, the client treats a request as unsafe unless it uses GET or HEAD.

The RFC says a user agent should ignore Safe: no on GET and HEAD responses because those methods are safe by definition.
sections.plainLanguage: A client may repeat a request automatically when the server marks it safe. GET and HEAD remain safe even if the server sends a Safe: no header.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the Safe header introduces no new security risks. It notes that allowing safe POST requests to be repeated without a warning may reduce pressure to use GET for form submissions, which the memo says has separate security risks.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says the header adds no new security risks. It may make POST easier to use for forms that should not be sent in a GET request.
